proposal_if_joined:
## What if I joined Wispr Flow?

A few opportunities I'd love to explore.

Before talking about what I could bring to Wispr Flow, I want to share what I've understood about the product, its market and where I think some interesting opportunities might exist.

I've been using Wispr Flow for the last four to five months, even before I discovered this hiring challenge. So this isn't only an outside perspective: I've experienced the product as a user.

### 1. The market is much bigger than voice-to-text

Think about how we interact with computers and mobile devices today. Whether we're using a desktop, a laptop or a smartphone, a significant part of that interaction still revolves around the keyboard. We type our thoughts, search queries, emails, instructions and responses.

What if expressing those thoughts could be as natural as speaking them?

I believe the opportunity for Wispr Flow goes beyond replacing typing. It is about making voice a primary interface for interacting with technology. The potential market is enormous, because almost everyone who uses a digital device needs to communicate something through it.

Wispr Flow has already made interesting progress in reaching consumers through creator-led marketing and UGC. I see that as a strong foundation to build on.

### 2. An opportunity in B2B: becoming the voice layer for SaaS

This is where my experience in the SaaS ecosystem makes me particularly curious. Over nearly five years, I've worked with consulting partners, technology partners and businesses implementing SaaS solutions. I've seen how software products evolve and how businesses adopt new ways of working.

One significant shift happening today is the evolution of software interfaces. Traditionally, users interacted with software through graphical interfaces: navigating menus, clicking buttons and typing information. With AI agents, MCP integrations and conversational interfaces, we're beginning to see a different way of interacting with software. Users increasingly want to express what they need in natural language, rather than navigate multiple screens.

I think this creates an interesting opportunity for Wispr Flow. Every SaaS product might eventually need a better way for its users to communicate with it through voice. Rather than every software company building and maintaining its own voice infrastructure, Wispr Flow could provide that capability.

Imagine Wispr Flow becoming the voice layer for:

- CRM platforms
- Customer support and helpdesk software
- HR management systems
- Project management tools
- Sales and productivity applications

### 3. Building technology partnerships

I'd love to explore partnerships with SaaS companies where Wispr Flow could be integrated into their products. There could be different partnership models:

- **Embedded or white-label integrations:** SaaS companies integrate Wispr Flow's voice capabilities natively into their applications.

- **Usage-based commercial partnerships:** partners pay based on voice usage, transcription volume or active users, creating a recurring revenue opportunity.

- **Technology and ecosystem partnerships:** working with SaaS companies to identify workflows where voice can significantly improve user productivity.

The idea is simple: instead of every SaaS company solving the voice-input problem on its own, Wispr Flow could become the technology partner that helps them deliver that experience.

### 4. The creative side I'd bring: creators and content

Creator-led growth is part of the job, and influencer marketing is one of the channels the India team is scaling. I come to it from both sides.

**As a creator,** I've been making content for years: a blog with 21 posts, a YouTube channel with 116 videos, writing on Medium, a Kindle book and a podcast. **As a collaborator,** I've worked with content creators and independent musicians on their shows, most closely Kaber Vasuki: I volunteered with friends to plan and run three concerts for an independent Tamil artist, end to end, and through that I learned how creators organize, what they struggle with, and how ticketed events run. **And I've seen distribution up close,** from Quora and blog experiments to affiliate marketing.

I'd love to bring that to regional-language creators in India, and test whether creators who already explain tools to their audience in their own mix of languages could make voice feel native.

[The blog](https://logeshr15.github.io/wisprportfolio/#/story/blog) · [Affiliate marketing](https://logeshr15.github.io/wisprportfolio/#/story/affiliate) · [The podcast](https://logeshr15.github.io/wisprportfolio/#/story/podcast) · [Independent music](https://logeshr15.github.io/wisprportfolio/#/story/indiemusic) · [The book](https://logeshr15.github.io/wisprportfolio/#/story/book)

## Why this interests me

I've experienced both sides of this ecosystem. I worked with affiliate marketing in my younger years and understood creator-led distribution, and I've spent nearly five years working with partners in the SaaS ecosystem. I've also been a user of Wispr Flow myself.

I see an opportunity to bring these experiences together: understanding how products reach users, how businesses adopt technology, and how partnerships can create new distribution and revenue channels.

These are some of the things I'd love to explore if I became part of the Wispr Flow team. Not as a list of promises, but as a starting point for conversations, experiments and opportunities.
dont_type_just_speak:
## Don't type. Just speak.

During my school days, I attended typing classes to improve my typing speed. Over the years I kept improving it, because I believed typing faster meant being more productive.

Today, my typing speed is **61 WPM**. But Wispr Flow shows my dictation speed is **152 WPM**. That's almost 2.5 times my typing speed.

**61** words per minute typing, at 100% accuracy
**152** words per minute speaking, with Wispr Flow
**2.5x** faster by voice
**Top 0.1%** for speed, as shown in Wispr Flow Insights

![Typing test result: 61 words per minute with 100% accuracy and no typos, a net speed of 61 WPM. Earlier attempts in the chart scored 9, 14 and 13 WPM.](https://logeshr15.github.io/wisprportfolio/images/typing-test.png)

My typing test: 61 WPM, 100% accuracy, no typos.

![Wispr Flow Insights: 152 words per minute, top 0.1%, 198 fixes made by Flow, 8,217 total words dictated, a one-day streak with a longest streak of 8 days.](https://logeshr15.github.io/wisprportfolio/images/wispr-insights.webp)

My Wispr Flow Insights: 152 words per minute, 8,217 words dictated, 198 fixes made by Flow, longest streak 8 days.

And here's a funny little story.

While building this entire portfolio, I barely had to touch my keyboard. I was mostly speaking my thoughts and letting Wispr Flow turn them into words. I love writing, but I realised we often confuse the action of typing with the actual process of writing. Writing is articulating your thoughts in a structured way. When I speak, I give more context than I do when I write, because typing is a physical limitation.

The typing scores of 9, 14 and 13 WPM you see in the chart? Those belong to my current manager's kid. He was impressed by my typing speed and wanted to learn how to type faster.

Maybe it's time I tell him something different.

You don't necessarily need to learn to type faster anymore. You can just speak.

That's the productivity shift I experienced with Wispr Flow.

Don't type. Just speak.

stories.title: The family business: helping my parents
stories.summary: I learned how a business works by helping my parents run theirs.
stories.text:
My parents run a family business: wholesale and manufacturing of home appliance covers. My father and mother run it together, and it ran from the first floor of our house.

I have helped with every part of it since I was a child. I watched how it worked and pitched in with the operations: sales, buying stock, and calling people to collect the money they owed.

That is how my childhood went.

stories.title: A blog nobody read
stories.summary: No views taught me what SEO means.
stories.text:
In 9th standard I was pulled in two directions. On one side was writing. On the other was e-commerce, because our family business was slowly thinking about selling online. I learned how to sell on Amazon, along with a lot of other things.

Then I started a blog, and nobody came. That is how I found out what SEO means. I took many online courses in digital marketing and social media marketing, and I learned that you have to build distribution, not just write. So I became very active on Quora, and Quora began sending lots of visitors to my website. It was my first experiment loop: try something, see what is working, and change it.

I ran several blogs. One of them is To Start A Startup. The others were mostly affiliate-marketing experiments where I posted things at random. They were experiments more than professional blogs, and I did not have a laptop, so I ran all of them from my mobile.

stories.title: Planning and running independent music concerts
stories.summary: Three concerts, planned and run end to end by friends, for the love of it.
stories.text:
I love independent music. Kaber Vasuki is one of my favourite independent artists, and he writes in Tamil. For his last three concerts, my friends and I volunteered and took care of the whole event, end to end, from the arrangements to running it on the day. It was event management, and I did it purely out of personal interest.

**Planning.** We handled the arrangements: getting entry cards ready for the guests who were coming, and organizing the seating.

**Executing.** On the day we ran the event: welcoming guests as they arrived, getting them seated, and meeting the fans as they came in.

**What I took away.** A network among creative people in independent music. A close look at how the scene works, and how hard it is for artists to organize events like these. How collaborating with creative people really works, and how ticketed events run. Through those connections I also went to performances by a few other independent artists.

I do not like to let go of any opportunity that comes my way.

If you are reading this, listen to Kaber's songs. If you understand Tamil, I am sure you will fall in love with the lyrics. One line is in my Instagram bio: “மிஞ்சிப்போனால் மரணம் என்றபோது வாழ்க்கை வாழ வெட்கப்படலாமா?” It means: if death is the most that can happen in the end, why be shy of living your life?

stories.title: Yercaud on foot: nearly 30,000 steps
stories.summary: No bike, no cab, no plan. Just walking.
stories.text:
After the event, I had one day left before heading back to Chennai. Instead of spending it resting, I decided to visit Yercaud.

I didn't rent a bike, book a cab or plan a public transport route. I decided to explore the place entirely on foot.

Nearly 30,000 steps later, I had experienced Yercaud in a way I probably wouldn't have if I had travelled by car.

I walked through its roads, took in the mountain views, observed people going about their lives and stopped to have conversations. I also got an opportunity to interact with local businesses and understand a little more about the people and business culture of Salem through my BNI connections.

What I particularly enjoy about walking is that it slows you down. You start noticing things you would otherwise pass by. The little details, the people, the conversations and the unexpected discoveries.

It was a wonderful solo-travel experience. No elaborate itinerary, no vehicle and no rush to get anywhere.

Just me, a lot of walking and a new place to explore.

stories.title: A free day, a fort, and a ride home with strangers
stories.summary: A trek, a crowd, and a ride home with people I had just met.
stories.text:
I had a free day before my meeting, so I decided to explore.

It was a weekend, and I took a train to Nashik. From there, I made my way to a fort for a trek. My original plan was simple: finish the trek and return by train or local transport.

But weekends have their own plans. The crowd slowed things down, and the trek took longer than I expected.

While trekking, I struck up conversations with a few strangers. By the time we reached the end, I somehow found myself hitchhiking back with them instead of following my original plan.

I didn't know these people before the trek. I hadn't planned this journey back either. Yet, we ended up sharing a ride, conversations and an experience I hadn't anticipated.

It was spontaneous, a little thrilling and genuinely fun.

Sometimes, the best part of exploring isn't the destination or the plan. It's the people you meet and the unexpected turns along the way.

stories.title: Advantage Vidarbha 2025: a few facts
stories.summary: A three-day industrial expo, with 100 stalls for micro and small enterprises.
stories.text:
Advantage Vidarbha 2025 was an industrial expo held in Nagpur from 7 to 9 February 2025. Here is what was reported about it.

- **Organiser:** the Association for Industrial Development (AID).
- **Venue:** the campus ground of Rashtrasant Tukadoji Maharaj University, Amravati Road, Nagpur.
- **Size:** more than 300 stalls, of which 100 were reserved for micro and small enterprises.
- **Who took part:** chief guests included Union Minister Nitin Gadkari and Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, and exhibitors included government bodies such as SEBI, the GST Department, the Department of Posts and the Government e-Marketplace (GeM).
- **Afterwards:** exhibitors reported a surge in visitor turnout, and several start-ups seeking investment reported meetings with potential investors.

For a small-business CRM, a room built for micro and small enterprises is the right place to be.
